title: Map furniture and map colour — Image Wiki
text:
Map furniture and map colour
  The standard parts of a map and what each is actually for, then how to pick a colour scheme from the shape of the data — and why a rainbow ruins ordered data.

  
    Termmap elements / cartographic colour
    Also calledmap furniture, north arrow, scale bar, legend, colour schemes, ColorBrewer
    Not the same asmap projection, chart colour palettes, brand colour
    Read9 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        The furniture, and what each piece is forColour, chosen by the shape of the dataWhy a rainbow lies about ordered dataInteractive maps are a family of designsCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Look at the bottom edge of a proper printed map. A scale bar. A line saying who surveyed it and when. A small crowded key. Nobody reads any of it — right up to the moment you need to know how far something is, or how old the information is, and then it is the only part of the sheet that matters.
The furniture, and what each piece is for
Campbell and Shin list the elements in the order they should be placed. Every one has a job, and it is worth knowing which are load-bearing.

Frame line — the box around everything on the page. Neat lines are the smaller boxes around individual elements, and must sit inside the frame line.
Mapped area — the map itself. Insets are secondary maps in their own neat lines: to show where this place sits in a bigger one, to reach a far-off piece like Alaska, or to blow up a corner too crowded to read.
Title — the largest type on the sheet, one line if you can manage it, top centre by default. It says what the map is for and who it is for.
Legend — a self-explanatory definition of every symbol used. Its real risk is size: strip out anything the reader already knows (state boundaries, an interstate shield) rather than shrinking the type until it is unreadable.
Source and date — small, plain, and prefixed with "Source:" so nobody mistakes it for a caption. This is the piece that lets a reader judge whether to trust the sheet at all.
Scale — a bar, a ratio, or words, and often all three, because readers arrive with different rulers. Deliberately not prominent; Campbell and Shin call it secondary.
Orientation — north up unless there is a reason, and if there is not a reason there should not be an arrow. Theirs is the sharpest line in the chapter: one of the commonest map errors is an overly large or overly ornate north arrow, because it only needs to be read once.




The left half of the bottom margin, Ordnance Survey One-Inch Sheet 90, Wensleydale, published 1961. Crown copyright expired; public domain. Click to enlarge.
All administration, all of it kept off the map. REVISION INFORMATION — fully revised 1959, major roads revised 1966 — is the most useful line on the sheet, because it tells you which parts are eight years stale. The PUBLIC RIGHTS OF WAY box admits how far the footpath survey actually got; the yellow box gives the National Park designation and its 1954 confirmation order; the index to adjoining sheets boxes 90 among its neighbours so you know which map to buy next.
There is no ornamental north arrow. Instead two small star diagrams of magnetic, grid and true north, a table of the grid-north difference measured at each corner of this sheet (0°23′E at the north-west corner, 0°07′W at the south-east), and a note that magnetic north was about 9°W in 1967, decreasing by about half a degree every six years. That is the only orientation fact a compass user can act on, and it sits in the margin where nobody trips over it.
The scale bars run in both directions from zero, subdivided finely to the left of it and coarsely to the right, so you can measure a short distance and a long one with the same edge of paper.


Some of this is convention rather than requirement, and conventions drift.



Willem Blaeu, Gviana sive Amazonvm Regio, Amsterdam, 1635. Public domain.
Every piece of furniture is here and every piece is decorated. The title sits in a carved cartouche; the scale bar has its own frame and gives two units, German and Gallic miles; the imprint sits in a third. Orientation is a compass rose with rhumb lines fanning across the whole sheet, plus SEPTENTRIO and MERIDIES lettered on the neat line — north and south spelled out because the arrow convention had not settled.
Then look at the middle: Parime Lacus, a large inland lake, drawn as confidently as the coast. It does not exist. Good furniture is not evidence.


Colour, chosen by the shape of the data
ColorBrewer's whole interface is one question — nature of your data — with three answers.

lowhigh0lossgainABCDEall five equal in weightSequentialrainfall, population, travel timeDiverginggain and loss around a real zeroQualitativeland use, soil class, party in power

The scheme follows the data, not your taste. Sequential for ordered low-to-high: one hue getting darker, so more ink means more of the thing. Diverging for data with a real midpoint: two hues meeting at a pale middle, which asserts that the middle means something. Qualitative for unordered categories: hues of roughly equal weight, so no class looks bigger than another.
The trap is the middle panel. A diverging scheme claims a critical value. Use it where zero, or the average, or "no change" is genuinely a boundary — never because you wanted two colours.


ColorBrewer then adds a number of classes — 3 to 12 — and three cross-cutting filters worth treating as constraints rather than preferences: colour-blind safe, print friendly, and photocopy safe. Mapbox says the same thing from the other side, that a significant portion of the population has limited colour vision and you should style accordingly, so a red-against-green scheme fails some of your readers outright. Print-friendly matters because press ink cannot reach every screen colour; photocopy-safe means the scheme still separates when it is flattened to grey. Mapbox's advice on quantity is the other half: 10 to 12 colours is a full palette for a whole map style, and matching saturation and lightness across the hues is what keeps it coherent.
Why a rainbow lies about ordered data

01000100looks like a boundarythe same values, no boundaryRainbow scaleno perceptual order; the hue jumps invent edgesPerceptually ordered scalelightness climbs with the value, evenly

The same numbers in both panels — one smooth surface, two gaussian bumps and a gentle ramp, no edges anywhere in the data.
Left, a rainbow scale. It has no perceptual order: nothing makes cyan feel greater than yellow, so the reader has to keep consulting the key. Worse, the hue steps are uneven, so where the value crosses certain points the colour lurches and the eye reads a contour line that is not there. The marked cell sits on one of those false edges.
Right, a scale whose lightness climbs steadily with the value. The same cell is unremarkable, because nothing happens there in the data. Darker means less, everywhere, and you can rank two patches without looking at the legend at all.


The same argument condemns the rainbow twice over: it invents boundaries, and it collapses in greyscale, because its lightness goes up and down.
Interactive maps are a family of designs
Mapbox is the bridge from print cartography to vector maps, and the structural difference is that a style is a set of rules applied at every zoom from z0 to z22. You are not designing one map. You are designing a family, and the sheet that works at city scale turns into a jumble at regional scale.
Their density rule is the useful one: features should not be styled just because the data is available at that zoom. Contour lines that read beautifully on a hillside become a grey smear at state level; every restaurant icon at city level is unreadable soup.
Labels are the hard part.

AshbyNortonMilbyAshbyNortonMilbyStowKirk HillWest BarrowEastgateMardendropped — would collideshown on the rightZoomed outthree names fit; the minor roads carry noneTwo zoom steps insame roads, four times the screen space per square mile

Identical geometry, two zooms. Left, only the three ranked places get names and the minor roads carry none — there is no room. Right, two zoom steps in, the same roads have four times the screen area per square mile, so smaller places can be named.
Then the constraint that never goes away: Marden cannot be labelled, because at this zoom its name would land on Stow's. A label must not collide at any zoom, and the zoom is continuous, so the renderer drops labels by rank as space runs out. Notice too that every name carries a faint halo of the background colour, which is how a label survives crossing a road.


Two more obligations that print does not have. Mobile screens reintroduce spatial restriction — a smaller viewport shows much less map at once, so fewer of your visual connections are ever on screen together. And attribution is contractual: Mapbox requires its logo plus "© Mapbox", "© OpenStreetMap" and an "Improve this map" link; you may restyle the attribution text to fit your theme so long as it stays legible, and you may not restyle the logo. On a printed export you cite it like a photograph, in text near the image.
Common mistakes

"Every map needs a north arrow and a scale bar." A north-up map at a familiar scale may need neither, and an ornate arrow is clutter with a job title.
"The legend explains it." A legend nobody reads explains nothing. Cut its rows before you cut its type size.
"Rainbow shows more detail." It shows more variation, in places the data does not vary. That is noise with good PR.
"Diverging looks nicer." It also asserts a threshold. If the midpoint is not real, you have invented a claim — the map version of the colour trap in When a chart lies.
"It looked right on my screen." Check it in grey, at the smallest size, and on the smallest device you support.


Checking a map's craft

Read the source line and the date. Missing? Stop there.
Title, scale, orientation: present where needed, absent where not, and none of them shouting.
Match the colour scheme to the data type. Ordered data on a rainbow is a defect.
If the scheme diverges, find the midpoint and ask what it means.
Screenshot it in greyscale and at half size. What disappears first?

              Everything on a map matters to somebody and it all has to fit in one plane. Five principles decide what wins — and the first real decision is which question the map is for.
            
          
        
          
            
              Hue, value and chroma
              A colour is not one thing. It is three independent dials — which colour it is, how light it is, and how far it sits from grey — and most arguments about colour are two people turning different dials.
            
          
        
          
            
              When a chart lies
              The dangerous chart is not the ugly one. It is the one where every number is correct and the picture still argues for something the numbers do not support.
            
          
        
          
            
              Legibility and readability
              Two different measurements that get treated as one — whether you can tell the characters apart, and whether you can get through a paragraph without effort.
